title: Behavioral Probes for Information Flow in LLM Swarms
claim: A node's reliance on external context rises with input relevance, while reliance on internal knowledge falls once context makes the answer inferable.
layout: 2 side-by-side density panels, (a) ECS and (b) PKS, dashed mean lines, stats boxes
description: Two side-by-side kernel-density plots with translucent histogram bars, sharing one four-color legend: blue for irrelevant (bubble), orange for related-but-unhelpful (rel), green for oracle and red for answer contexts. Panel (a), ECS, shows the four distributions shifting rightward in order, from a mean near 0.1 for bubble to about 0.33 for answer. The green and red curves overlap heavily at the right. Panel (b), PKS, shows heavily overlapping right-skewed curves. The red answer curve is shifted left and sharply peaked near 1.2, and the other curves peak around 1.5 to 2. Dashed vertical lines mark each group's mean. Annotation boxes in the upper right list the mean and standard deviation of each group. The eye goes first to the clearly separated ECS peaks, then to the red PKS peak. Captions (a) ECS and (b) PKS sit below the panels.
caption: Node-level response patterns under four context conditions: irrelevant (bubble), related but unhelpful (rel), oracle denotes inverse relational evidence that is sufficiently informative for reverse inference, and answer denotes context directly containing the answer. Curves and translucent bars show score densities, dashed vertical lines mark group means, and the annotation boxes report mean and standard deviation. Overall, ECS increases with context relevance, while PKS decreases when the answer can be inferred from the provided context.
abstract: Most existing approaches to LLM swarm optimization are utility-driven, focusing on final task utility while leaving the processing, integration, and reliance of information within individual interactions largely implicit. To address this, we study LLM swarm interactions from an information-flow-based view and introduce behavioral probes to quantify information flow patterns. Specifically, we repurpose External Context Score (ECS) and Parametric Knowledge Score (PKS)---originally designed for hallucination analysis---to measure a node's external-context dependence and parametric-knowledge dependence, respectively. Across controlled and realistic swarm settings, we observe consistent patterns: ECS increases with input relevance and distinguishes useful multi-source contributions, while PKS decreases as informative context accumulates. Building on this heuristic interpretation, we demonstrate how these probes can complement utility-driven structure optimization in two controlled applications. Probe-guided node pruning reduces redundant communication and token consumption, and probe-guided reasoning-path search accelerates convergence compared to utility-only baselines. Our empirical results suggest that behavioral probes can make the internal information flow of LLM swarms observable and serve as effective auxiliary signals for structure optimization.
